description: Somos un equipo creativo y apasionado por la tecnología, nos gusta crear soluciones mediante la programación y la robótica aplicadas a la vida real
summary: What happens to the brave robotic explorers and spacecraft that paved the way for humanity on the Moon and Mars once their missions end? They may be abandoned or retired due to weight constraints and technical limits, but they are never forgotten. Our project, SPACE COWBOY: Historic Probe Rescue, is an interactive educational video game built in Scratch featuring a retro 16-bit aesthetic inspired by classic Super Nintendo (SNES) games. Taking on the role of a Space Cowboy on a historical preservation mission, players travel across Mars and the Moon to locate, rescue, and learn the real science behind four iconic NASA spacecraft: Viking 1 and InSight on Mars, and Surveyor 6 alongside the Apollo 11 Lunar Module "Eagle" on the Moon. Instead of reading a static textbook, children and youth experience aerospace history through dynamic platformer stages and a thrilling Martian atmospheric entry sequence connecting Viking 1's orbiter and lander. Upon reaching each spacecraft, an interactive data window displays authentic NASA specifications—including mass, dimensions, power systems (such as SNAP-19 RTGs and solar panels), scientific payloads (seismometers, heat probes, robotic arms), and the exact engineering reasons why each vehicle remained in space. Built 100% manually by our team without Artificial Intelligence, it is real space history and science you can play, explore, and preserve.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

SPACE COWBOY: Historic Probe Rescue is an educational and interactive video game developed in Scratch with a 16-bit Super Nintendo visual style designed to spread knowledge about historic probes, landers, and equipment left behind after completing their assigned missions.

The player controls a Space Cowboy across two planetary bodies and four historical levels:

  • Mission 1 – Mars (Viking 1 & InSight):
    • Viking 1 (Launched August 20, 1975): Performed NASA's first truly successful landing on Mars. Its level includes a Martian atmospheric entry sequence between discovering the orbiter (abandoned August 7, 1980, after running out of attitude-control propellant) and the lander (which stopped communicating on November 11, 1982, after a faulty command).
    • InSight (Launched May 5, 2018): A platformer level across the Martian crust to find the lander that investigated "marsquakes" and subsurface heat flow using its 1.8-meter robotic arm until its mission concluded on December 15, 2022.
    • Surveyor 6 (Launched November 7, 1967): A lunar platformer stage where the player reaches the first spacecraft ever launched from the lunar surface after capturing over 30,000 photographs.
    • Apollo 11 Lunar Module "Eagle" (July 1969): A platformer level set at the historic landing site of Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, explaining how the Early Apollo Scientific Experiment Package (EASEP) and module stages were left behind due to strict weight and safety requirements.
  • Interactive Information Windows: Reaching each spacecraft triggers an interactive retro window detailing official NASA specs, onboard instruments, and why the hardware remained on the surface or in orbit.
2. What benefits does it have?
  • Educational & STEAM Learning: Promotes active learning in space history, physics, aerospace engineering, and coding through interactive play.
  • Scientific & Technical Literacy: Explains real-world concepts including launch mass constraints, radioisotope thermoelectric generators (SNAP-19 RTGs), solar power arrays, planetary seismology, and atmospheric entry.
  • Historical Preservation: Teaches young generations to value the pioneering robotic and crewed missions (1967–2022) that made modern space exploration possible.
  • Universal Accessibility: Developed in Scratch so anyone can play for free in a web browser or offline with intuitive controls tailored for children and youth.
3. What do you hope to achieve? (Expected Impact)

Our goal is to bring the history and engineering of space exploration closer to children and young people, especially in communities with limited access to aerospace museums or science labs.

  • Spark scientific and technological vocations through the appeal of classic SNES-style arcade gaming.
  • Encourage equal participation of girls and boys in STEAM fields through a barrier-free digital experience.
  • Show that retired probes are not mere "space junk," but enduring scientific monuments across the Solar System.
4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
  • Programming Environment and Language: Scratch (visual block-based coding for platformer physics, lunar/Martian gravity, atmospheric entry mechanics, and interactive UI windows).
  • Visual Design and Graphic Assets: Original 16-bit Pixel Art inspired by classic Super Nintendo (SNES) titles and official archival imagery from the NASA Image and Video Library.
  • Official Scientific Data Sources: NASA Science Mission Directorate (Viking 1, InSight, Surveyor 6), NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA – Apollo 11 Lunar Module), and Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL).
  • Artificial Intelligence Disclosure: No Artificial Intelligence tools were used (0% AI usage) in the development of the code, pixel art, or documentation for this project. All research, writing, artwork, and programming were completed entirely by hand by our team members.
5. How is your project creative?
  • Original "Space Cowboy" Preservationist Concept: Turns planetary archaeology into an action-packed rescue adventure across the Moon and Mars.
  • 16-Bit SNES Aesthetic Meets Real NASA Data: Blends 1990s retro gaming charm with authentic engineering specifications from NASA Langley and JPL.
  • Mission-Specific Gameplay: Combines atmospheric entry gameplay with surface platforming tailored to the actual historical profile of each spacecraft.
6. What factors did your team consider?
  • Historical & Scientific Accuracy: Manual verification of spacecraft masses (3,527 kg for Viking-B, 360 kg for InSight, 1,008.3 kg for Surveyor 6), launch dates, launch vehicles (Titan IIIE-Centaur, Atlas-Centaur, Saturn V), and scientific instruments.
  • Pedagogical Clarity: Presenting technical engineering data in concise, engaging interactive windows inside the game.
  • Accessibility & Motivation: Although our team is deeply involved in the STEAM world, we noticed that many children and youth know very little about the historic probes still resting on the Moon and Mars, while their passion for video games continues to grow. Inspired by our love for space exploration and hands-on learning at our school, we created this interactive game so any child can enjoy and learn real space science while playing.
